finding: On a benchmark built to block memorization, the best LLM equation-discovery system solves under a third of problems.
numbers: 239 problems, 4 domains (LSR-Transform 111 transformed Feynman problems; LSR-Synth chem, bio, physics, material science). Best symbolic accuracy: LLM-SR with GPT-4o-mini 31.53% on LSR-Transform; best synthetic-domain symbolic accuracy about 28% (LaSR, material science).
quote: best-performing system so far achieves only 31.5%
limits: Symbolic accuracy judged by GPT-4o (94.6% agreement with humans on a sample). Table text is garbled in PDF extraction, so per-cell values for synthetic domains are approximate.
agent_relevance: Rediscovery of a known law is much harder once the textbook form is hidden; a schema step that reproduces a discovery must be tested on disguised problems, not famous ones.

finding: Famous Feynman equations are recited from memory, not discovered. The same physics rewritten as a different but equivalent target (solve for another variable) is much harder at equal expression size.
numbers: Fig 1 and Fig 4: Llama-3.1-8B sampling on 100 Feynman problems shows sharp early error drops and lower symbolic error than on LSR-Transform and LSR-Synth. The gap persists even for expressions of 0-15 nodes.
limits: Aggregated over methods and backbones. Shows memorization is a confound, not that no discovery occurs.
agent_relevance: Any test of the agent on named historical laws is contaminated. Use counterfactual or transformed versions (guardrails G3, G8).

finding: A classic genetic-programming baseline with no domain words matches LLMs on fit but not on getting the right formula.
numbers: Table 3, equal evaluation budget. PySR on LSR-Transform: symbolic 8.11%, numeric Acc0.1 56.76%. LLM-SR best: 31.53% / 39.64%. PySR symbolic accuracy 0% on chemistry and biology; 4.54% on LSR-Synth physics.
limits: PySR run at default settings. Numeric accuracy is not the same as the right law.
agent_relevance: Fitting the data (G3) is not rediscovery. Names and context help the model reach the right form; the checker must test form, not only error.

finding: Plain prompting with no data loop is nearly useless; the search loop and data feedback do the work. All methods degrade out of domain.
numbers: Direct prompting (data-blind): best symbolic accuracy 7.21% on LSR-Transform (GPT-4o-mini) and 0% on most synthetic domains. LLM-SR gets the lowest NMSE in-domain and out-of-domain; direct prompting is worst. Symbolic accuracy correlates positively with out-of-domain Acc0.1.
limits: Backbone ordering odd: GPT-4o-mini and Llama-8B beat GPT-3.5-turbo; authors speculate less opinionated models explore better.
agent_relevance: Supports a generate-test-revise loop over one-shot answers. Held-out extrapolation is the useful check.

finding: LLM-SR (equation skeleton by LLM, constants fitted by optimizer, experience buffer) beats classical symbolic regression with far fewer evaluations.
numbers: About 2.5K iterations vs 2M+ for baselines. E. coli growth out-of-domain NMSE about 0.0037 for LLM-SR, above 1 for other methods. Baselines: GPlearn, NeSymReS, E2E, DSR, uDSR, PySR.
limits: Four problems, some custom-made; authors' own benchmark. Later benchmarks (LLM-SRBench) show a much lower ceiling.
agent_relevance: Splitting the hypothesis (LLM, structure) from the fit (code, constants) matches the schema rule that code decides.

finding: Ablation on Oscillation 2 shows each loop part matters; removing the iterative data loop or the separate fitter hurts most.
numbers: Without iterative refinement: NMSE 1.01e-1 in-domain, 1.81e-1 out-of-domain. Without skeleton+optimizer (LLM writes constants too): 3.78e-1 / 3.75e-1. Removing the problem description (no prior) and removing code form also hurt, the latter less.
limits: One problem, GPT-3.5 backbone, small N of runs.
agent_relevance: Essential steps in the loop: fit from real output, keep a buffer of best attempts, keep domain words. Directly answers the ablation question in SUBFIELDS.

finding: The authors detect recitation on Feynman problems and move to custom problems.
numbers: LLM-SR reached low error in under 20 iterations on Feynman problems. Mixtral perplexity on Feynman equation tokens was clearly lower than on their new problems.
limits: Perplexity is indirect evidence; no training-data audit.
agent_relevance: Early exact fit with little data is a recitation alarm. A cheap check the program can run.

finding: A physics-inspired recursive method (dimensional analysis, symmetry, separability, neural-net fit) rediscovered all 100 Feynman equations; the prior best public tool solved 71.
numbers: 100/100 vs 71/100 (Eureqa). Noise tolerance reported per equation.
limits: Noise-free or low-noise data; the equations are textbook ones, chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Modern successor to BACON: gains came from exploiting structure (separable, symmetric) after a cheap test, not blind search.

finding: Pareto-optimal search over complexity and fit made the method far more noise-robust.
numbers: 73 of 100 baseline problems solved at noise level 10^-1 relative; typically 1-3 orders of magnitude more robust than v1. In a 2-hour limit v1 solved 5 of the hard equations; v2 solved all of them plus 4 other open ones. 80% of ten extra distributions solved.
limits: Authors' own comparison; Gaussian noise only.
agent_relevance: Keep a frontier of candidates by (error, simplicity), not one best (see MDL link).

finding: Independent large benchmark: AI Feynman is best on noise-free Feynman data but brittle with noise and on real-world data.
numbers: Noise-free ground truth: AIFeynman exact solutions 53% of the time, nearly twice the next method (GP-GOMEA 27%). At noise above 0.01, DSR, gplearn, AFP_FE and AFP recover more. On black-box tasks AIFeynman ranked below FFX and DSR (p <= 6.1e-5).
limits: Ground-truth set is Feynman plus Strogatz ODEs (130 datasets), 10 repeats; method designed for physics-symmetry problems.
agent_relevance: Independent replication cut the headline from 100/100 to 53% noise-free: author-tuned results shrink under third-party testing. Same warning for LLM papers.

finding: For real-world regression, genetic programming with parameter fitting or semantic search beats newer deep methods; for exact recovery under noise, deep and GP methods perform similarly.
numbers: Four of the top five black-box methods (Operon, SBP-GP, FEAT, EPLEX) are GP-based; 14+ SR methods, 122 black-box and 130 ground-truth problems.
limits: Benchmark conclusions depend on the solution definition (symbolic equivalence).
agent_relevance: No single search style wins. Mix methods and score by the same checker.

finding: Adding an LLM-learned library of text concepts to genetic search gave a modest rise in exact solves on the 100 Feynman equations.
numbers: Exact solve: PySR 59/100; LaSR with Llama3-8B 67, 69, 71 at LLM-call rates 1%, 5%, 10%; LaSR with GPT-3.5 at 1%: 72/100.
limits: Same hyperparameters as PySR; Feynman set is memorized by LLMs, so part of gain may be recall. Gain +8 to +13 equations, single run per cell.
agent_relevance: Concept reuse across candidate hypotheses is a small, cheap gain; it is the nearest thing to a learned-lesson operator.

finding: Ablations: stripping variable names hurts most; the concept library speeds convergence.
numbers: Solved = MSE under 1e-11 within 40 iterations. Removing variable names gives a substantial drop; no concept library converges slower, a gap that widens at concept-guidance above 0.1%.
limits: Ablation on a subset; MSE criterion differs from exact match.
agent_relevance: Meaning in names carries real signal, matching LLM-SR and PhysGym results.

finding: Three baseline LLM agents (ReAct, Plan+Execute, Hypothesizer) fail most multi-step discovery tasks, even easy ones.
numbers: 24 main tasks of 120 total, 5 seeds each. Task completion, averages: ReAct 0.38 easy, 0.18 normal, 0.18 challenge. Plan+Execute 0.18, 0.18, 0.15. Hypothesizer 0.28, 0.23, 0.08. Knowledge scores: ReAct 0.25, 0.14, 0.10; Hypothesizer 0.34, 0.19, 0.08.
limits: Early-2024 base models; column order read from the table layout.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis-first scaffold helped easy knowledge score but not hard tasks. Scaffold shape alone is not enough.

finding: Expert human scientists did much better than the agents on the same tasks.
numbers: Up to 11 practicing scientists, 1 hour limit, same seed. Average completion 66%, explanatory knowledge 55%; 11 of 16 tasks above 60% completion.
limits: Humans saw one seed with the 2D interface; no retries; small N per task.
agent_relevance: A human baseline for discovery loops. Gap on challenge tasks (agents 0.08-0.18 vs human 0.66 overall) is the headroom.

finding: Counterfactual law shifts (altered known laws) in interactive systems separate strong reasoning models from weak ones, with GPT-5 far ahead.
numbers: 324 tasks, 12 physics domains, 11 LLMs. Overall symbolic accuracy: GPT-5 75.9%, Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4%, GPT-5-mini 53.1%, o4-mini 47.8%, DeepSeek-R1 43.4%; GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V3 under 10% (5.1-8.9%).
limits: Four runs per cell; symbolic equivalence graded by an LLM judge (98.3% agreement with humans).
agent_relevance: Reasoning-model strength matters more than scaffold in this test; G11 caution on cost: GPT-5 uses about 19k tokens per task vs 2-3k for weak models.

finding: Discovery collapses as the system gets complex and with tiny noise.
numbers: Hardest setting (complex system, hard shift): GPT-5 40.3%, Gemini-2.5-pro 16.7%, all other reasoning models under 6%. Noise of 0.0001 alone cut accuracy 12-16% vs noise-free; accuracy fell steadily to noise 0.1.
limits: Noise added to a clean simulator; real data noise may differ.
agent_relevance: Add a noise-sensitivity probe: an answer that flips with tiny noise is not a law (G3).

finding: A code interpreter helps weak models and slightly hurts strong ones by cutting exploration short.
numbers: Weak models gained: GPT-4.1 5.8% to 18.9%, GPT-4.1-mini 5.1% to 14.7%, DeepSeek-V3 8.9% to 13.3%. Strong models fell: GPT-5-mini 53.1 to 48.1, Gemini-2.5-flash 50.6 to 40.9, o4-mini 47.8 to 45.1, Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4 to 63.7. Budget sweep: harm appears when code budget goes from zero to one.
limits: Cause (premature exploit) is inferred from exploration-rate traces for four models.
agent_relevance: Tools do not simply help. Gate tool use behind an explicit explore-first budget, in line with G12.

finding: An agent that writes its own data-analysis code and keeps long-horizon experience beats LLM-as-proposer pipelines.
numbers: On LSR-Synth: GPT-OSS-120B backbone Acc0.01 63.57%, Acc0.001 49.35%; absolute margins of 6% to 35% over baselines across 4 disciplines. Ablation (GPT): no data-analysis tool 35.66/16.28; no experience buffer 57.36/41.86; no top-k 58.14/41.86. Qwen: no experience buffer 35.66 vs 49.09 full.
limits: Authors' own system; three-run averages.
agent_relevance: Data analysis before proposing and a memory of top candidates are the two ablated essentials. Supports an inspect-data step before generation.

finding: Even the LSR-Transform benchmark leaks by memory, per these authors.
numbers: Footnote: nearly 50% of LSR-Transform problems reached small error after the first iteration.
limits: A footnote claim, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Second independent flag of memorization on transformed known laws.

finding: Removing prior information (context, variable descriptions, variable names) steadily lowers success; priors matter more for hard tasks.
numbers: Four prior levels. o4-mini 62.89% to 41.24% when context removed; success at lowest prior level about half of the highest for all models. Top models fall from 66% to 31%. Claude 3.7 Sonnet had its biggest drop from level 3 to 4 (variable names removed).
limits: Success on individual problems is non-monotonic: some solved only at low priors and failed at high priors.
agent_relevance: Names and context are a double-edged resource; recall can mislead. Test the schema with names stripped (anonymized variables) as a control.

finding: A concept-driven symbolic system rediscovered Newton's second law, energy conservation and universal gravitation from 46 simulated mechanics experiments with no prior physics.
numbers: 46 experiments with noise; about 90 concepts and 50 general laws on average; max 1200 trials, about 48 hours per run.
limits: Simulated noisy data; the authors supplied a plausible-reasoning framework and concept-proposal design; one lab.
agent_relevance: Closest modern relative of BACON and KEKADA across several experiments: reuse of concepts across experiments, era control.

finding: Combining symbolic regression with a logic prover that checks candidate formulas against background theory re-found Kepler's third law from few data points; it did not recover time dilation from data but picked the best-generalising formula.
numbers: Kepler data sets of 8 planets and a 20-point set. Langmuir adsorption also treated. Reasoning-error metrics rank candidates that fit equally well.
limits: Prior axioms were elicited by hand per problem. Few problems.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G3: break ties among equally fitting candidates with a derivation check, not more fit.

source: Ma et al. (2024) LLM and Simulation as Bilevel Optimizers
finding: A generate-simulate-refine loop (LLM proposes, simulator scores, outer loop revises) beat CoT and other LLM baselines, and still works on an imaginary law that cannot be memorized.
numbers: Gap over 50% on the hardest constitutive-law tasks (paper wording); also tested on symbolic regression vs 14 SRBench baselines and 3 pre-trained baselines, and molecule design. Imaginary constitutive law test with materials changed by 50%, 30%, 20%.
limits: GPT-4-turbo backbone; few tasks. Other LLMs (Mixtral) also work.
agent_relevance: Loop with real feedback again the winning pattern.

finding: Data-driven discovery workflows taken from published papers remain hard: best agent about 25%.
numbers: 264 real tasks across 6 domains plus 903 synthetic tasks; best system 25%. Biology 0%, engineering 7%, economics 25%, sociology 23%.
limits: Metric is facet-based hypothesis match scored by an LLM.
agent_relevance: Fits G12: where success is near zero (biology 0%), search will not help.

finding: With an LLM whose cutoff is before 2024, an agent can recover the core of new chemistry hypotheses when given the right inspirations, thanks to a retrieve, compose, rank decomposition.
numbers: Benchmark of 51 papers from 2024. Hit ratio of ground-truth inspirations kept after screening to top 4% of a corpus: GPT-4o 83.7%, Llama-3.1-70B 83.0%, Llama-3.1-8B 43.5%. Top 20%: GPT-4o 96.7%.
limits: Rediscovery of already-published hypotheses with expert-annotated inspirations; not proof of new discovery; ranking uses LLM scoring.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of the right analogy source is the bottleneck, not combining. Links to analogy and recombination subfields.

finding: Ten generative-model environments test experiment design and model revision; no tested LLM does well at either.
numbers: Larger models (32B) beat smaller (7B) and closed models beat open ones, but all struggled. Experimental design scored by expected information gain.
limits: Only abstract-level findings read for this note.
agent_relevance: Experiment choice is a separate weak step; see value-of-information link.

finding: BACON.3 found constancies and trends in tabulated data with a few heuristics and rediscovered classic laws.
numbers: Abstract: ideal gas law, Kepler's third law, Coulomb's law, Ohm's law, Galileo's pendulum and constant-acceleration laws.
limits: Abstract only (paper PDF not reachable this session). Data were handed over clean, with the right variables chosen by the programmer.
agent_relevance: The original proof that a few cheap heuristics can reproduce a law; later critiques show how much was pre-supplied.

source: Qin and Simon (1990) Laboratory replication of scientific discovery processes
finding: Human participants given unlabeled planetary distance and period data: a minority found Kepler's law.
numbers: Search-result summary: 4 of 14 subjects found the same law Kepler did; a fifth came close.
limits: Seen only in a search summary; original not opened. Small N.
agent_relevance: Human success rate (about 29%) is a useful bar for any agent claiming rediscovery.

source: Heeffer (2021) Promises and disappointments of AI for scientific discovery
finding: Critique: BACON did not use the data available to the original discoverers, and induction from observation does not match how the historical laws were found; case studies are the sine law of refraction and Kepler's third law.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Seen only in a search summary; page returned 403 on fetch.
agent_relevance: Reconstruction proves sufficiency of a method on cleaned data, not that the historical path was followed.
